text: John Harry Dunning OBE (26 June 1927 – 29 January 2009) was a British economist widely recognized as the father of the field of international business. He conducted research on the economics of international direct investment and the multinational enterprise from the 1950s until his death. In the 1980s, he developed the eclectic paradigm, also known as the OLI-Model or Framework, as an extension of Internalization theory, which remains the dominant theoretical perspective for studying international business activities, particularly foreign direct investment and multinational enterprises. His first book, *American Investment in British Manufacturing Industry* (1958), is considered the first seminal work in the field. Dunning was born in Sandy, Bedfordshire on 26 June 1927. At age 15, he took a junior clerical position with S.E. Higgins & Co., a London insurance brokerage, and shortly after began working in London with Banco de Bilbao, where he studied English, Elements of Banking and Accounting, and Foreign Exchange. As World War II ended, he joined the Royal Navy and was posted to Sri Lanka (then called Ceylon) in 1945. After completing his naval service, he earned his BSc in Economics from University College London. He joined the Department of Economics at the University of Southampton in 1952 as an assistant lecturer and became a senior lecturer in 1962. In 1953, he began research on American firms' foreign direct investment into the UK and its impact on UK economic performance, leading to the 1958 book. In 1964, he was appointed Foundation Chair of Economics at the University of Reading. During his leadership of the economics department at Reading, he published key work on the eclectic paradigm. Along with other Reading colleagues, he developed the theory of the multinational enterprise, which significantly influenced international business academia, establishing what is known as the Reading School of International Business. Two institutions were greatly shaped by Dunning: the University of Reading, which he founded as a center for theoretical and empirical research on multinational enterprises, and the Academy of International Business (AIB), which he led as President and Dean of the Fellows. He recruited notable scholars such as Mark Casson, Peter Buckley, John Cantwell, Bob Pierce, Rajneesh Narula, Klaus Meyer, and Sarianna Lundan, and supervised several dozen doctoral students, including Professor James H. Landi and Jeremy Clegg. He also established a doctoral program in international business at Rutgers University in New Jersey. Dunning was a founder of the European International Business Academy. Since August 2008, the Henley Business School at the University of Reading has housed the John H. Dunning Centre for International Business, formerly the Centre for International Business and Strategy (CIBS), which was renamed in 2008 in his honor and is regarded as one of the world’s leading research centers in international business. Notable members of the Centre include Alan Rugman, Mark Casson, and Rajneesh Narula, one of Dunning’s doctoral students and founding director of the Centre. Dunning died on 29 January 2009, a year after being diagnosed with cancer. In the same year, the *Journal of International Business Studies*, the most prestigious academic journal in the field, stated that Dunning is widely recognized as the father of international business and noted that his influence is evident through a Google Scholar citation count exceeding 30,000—more than any other scholar in the field.
